facts.claim: In the United States, Regulation B under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act bars a lender, business credit included, from discriminating against an applicant on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status or age, among other prohibited bases, and from taking any of them into account when scoring creditworthiness; since 21 July 2026 it also says the Act does not use the “effects test”, which judges a rule by its outcomes alone. The rule as the eCFR prints it; not legal advice.

Hardt, Price and Srebro (2016) proposed equal opportunity: among the people who would qualify, each group should be turned down equally often. They show how to adjust any trained model to meet it, with a bar per group.

Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2016) proved that three natural fairness conditions for risk scores cannot all hold at once, except in narrow special cases such as a perfect predictor or equal base rates.
Chouldechova (2017) showed that when two groups’ base rates differ, a score with equal precision in both cannot also have equal false-positive and false-negative rates in both.

Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan’s Fairness and Machine Learning (MIT Press, 2023) warns that removing the group field can be ineffective and even harmful: other fields often encode it, and the model finds that encoding instead.

Kusner, Loftus, Russell and Silva (2017) define counterfactual fairness: a decision is fair to a person if it would stay the same in a world where they belonged to another group, which needs a causal model of how the fields came about.

Buolamwini and Gebru (2018) tested three commercial systems that guess gender from a face photo: darker-skinned women were the group they got wrong most, up to 34.7% of the time, while lighter-skinned men were never wrong more than 0.8% of the time.

NIST’s 2019 test of face recognition systems (Grother, Ngan and Hanaoka) found that across demographic groups, wrong matches often differed 10 to over 100 times, while missed matches mostly differed less than 3 times, and asked for both rates to be reported for each group at the bar the system uses.

The CFPB’s 2014 method paper explains that lenders outside mortgages generally may not ask an applicant’s race, so for its fair-lending reviews it estimates race and ethnicity from the applicant’s surname and the census block group (a small neighbourhood) where they live, which beats either one alone.
